bullets: Victorian society had a severe **double standard**: men’s sexual behaviour was excused; women were shamed, excluded, and often unable to work or marry.
Women had little legal or economic power; **marriage** was often their only security, so it worked like a transaction.
**Illegitimate children** could not inherit titles or land: hence the irony of the ending.
Rossetti gives a voice to a woman whom society silenced, inviting sympathy. Her religious faith shaped ideas of sin, but also of compassion and forgiveness.
The poem uses the **ballad** tradition (stories of seduction and betrayal), which links it to folk song.

callouts.p: Do not just say ‘women had no rights’. Say: because a ‘fallen woman’ was considered ‘unclean’, the speaker’s defiant voice is radical; Rossetti, who worked with such women, lets her accuse the lord and Kate rather than repent.

core.p: Christina Rossetti (1830–1894) was a devout **Anglican** poet. From about 1859 she volunteered at the **St Mary Magdalene Penitentiary in Highgate**, a refuge for ‘fallen women’ (women who had sex outside marriage, often prostitutes or seduced servants). Cousin Kate was published in 1862 in Goblin Market and Other Poems.

bullets: **Conflict type**: between two women (cousins), between classes, between the sexes, and between the speaker and society.
**Big message**: Victorian society’s double standards and class power destroy women; women are set against each other by men.
**Perspective**: first-person dramatic monologue, addressing first the reader, then Kate, then the son.
core.p: A working-class girl is seduced by a lord, lives with him as his mistress, and is then abandoned when he marries her cousin Kate. She contrasts Kate’s respectable, wealthy life with her own disgrace, argues that her own love was truer, and claims that she would have refused him. Finally she triumphs: she has a son, while Kate has no child, so the lord has no heir.

bullets: **Change of addressee** structures the poem: the reader (stanzas 1–2), Kate (3–5), the son (6).
**Tone develops** from lament to bitterness to anger to triumph.
**Rhetorical questions** in stanzas 1 and 4 challenge the reader.
Regular rhyme suggests control: she has rehearsed this argument; it may also reflect the rigid social rules that trap her.
core.p: Six stanzas of eight lines with a **ballad** rhythm (alternating tetrameter and trimeter) and a regular rhyme on alternate lines (ABCBDBEB). The steady, song-like form contains raw emotion.

bullets: **Gender power**: the lord ‘lured’, ‘wore’, ‘changed’, ‘chose’ and ‘bound’: all active verbs; the women are objects.
**Conflict between women**: men’s power sets cousins against each other.
**Society vs individual**: ‘The neighbours call…’ shows communal judgement.
**Revenge**: the son becomes a weapon; compare Blake’s poisoned apple.

callouts.p: Is Kate a villain or another victim? She is ‘bound’ with a ring and probably ‘frets’ about her childlessness. A perceptive answer suggests both women are trapped by the same lord and the same society.

essays.q: Compare how social class creates conflict in Cousin Kate and The Class Game.
essays.text: In Cousin Kate class power is literal and destructive. The ‘great lord’ who ‘lured’ the ‘cottage maiden’ to his ‘palace’ has the active verbs, while she is reduced to a ‘plaything’ that he ‘changed… like a glove’, a simile that makes her as disposable as an accessory. The neighbours’ judgement, ‘an outcast thing’, shows that Victorian society punished the woman rather than the lord, a double standard that Rossetti saw at first hand in her work with ‘fallen women’. Casey’s speaker is also judged by others, but for how she speaks and lives rather than for a sexual ‘sin’, and she answers back directly. Where Rossetti contains the speaker’s anger within a regular ballad rhyme scheme, Casey uses dialect and a repeated challenging question to the listener, so the working-class voice itself becomes the weapon. The endings show the difference most clearly: Rossetti’s speaker can only triumph indirectly, through a son who could one day ‘wear his coronet’, which keeps her trapped in the lord’s values of land and title; Casey’s speaker ends by celebrating her class rather than wanting to rise out of it.
essays.thesis: Both poems give a voice to a working-class woman judged by her ‘betters’, but Rossetti’s speaker has been ruined by class power and can only fight back through her son, while Casey’s speaker rejects middle-class judgement outright and takes pride in her class.
why: Conceptual contrast of indirect versus direct resistance.

mistakes.r: The speaker is the abandoned cousin; Kate is addressed.
She blames the lord and society too; arguably Kate is also a victim.
Rossetti was devout but compassionate; she gives the woman a voice to expose double standards.
mistakes.w: Rossetti approved of the speaker’s sin.

mistakes.r: It is ambiguous: triumphant, but also bitter and possessive.

poem.how: Six eight-line stanzas. Watch how the speaker addresses the reader first, then Kate directly, then her son.

stanzas.label: Stanza 1: innocence
lines: I was a cottage maiden
Hardened by sun and air,
Contented with my cottage mates,
Not mindful I was fair.
Why did a great lord find me out,
And praise my flaxen hair?
Why did a great lord find me out
To fill my heart with care?

notes.n: Past tense: she **was** innocent and is no longer. ‘Cottage maiden’ signals her working-class, rural status and virginity.
notes.w: I was a cottage maiden

notes.n: Physically strong and working outdoors: natural, honest, not a delicate lady.
notes.w: Hardened by sun and air,

notes.n: She was unaware of her beauty: innocence. The lord’s attention made her beauty a danger.
notes.w: Not mindful I was fair.

notes.n: **Repeated rhetorical question**: anguish and accusation. ‘Great lord’ shows the vast **class power** gap; ‘find me out’ sounds predatory, like hunting.
notes.w: Why did a great lord find me out,

notes.n: ‘Care’ means sorrow and worry. The ballad-like **ABCBDBEB** rhyme (air / fair / hair / care) gives a song-like, lamenting tone.
notes.w: To fill my heart with care?

stanzas.label: Stanza 2: seduction and shame
lines: He lured me to his palace home—
Woe's me for joy thereof—
To lead a shameless shameful life,
His plaything and his love.
He wore me like a silken knot,
He changed me like a glove;
So now I moan, an unclean thing,
Who might have been a dove.

notes.n: ‘Lured’ suggests bait and a trap: she presents herself as a victim of manipulation, not a willing sinner.
notes.w: He lured me

notes.n: **Oxymoronic** mix of woe and joy, with archaic, ballad-like diction. Dashes show emotional interruption.
notes.w: Woe's me for joy thereof—

notes.n: **Juxtaposition**: shameless at the time (she was in love), shameful now in society’s eyes. Also suggests the lord was shameless and she bears the shame.
notes.w: shameless shameful

notes.n: Possessive ‘His’ repeated: she was his object. ‘Plaything’ shows he treated her as a toy.
notes.w: His plaything and his love.

notes.n: **Similes** of clothing: she was a fashion accessory, worn and discarded.
notes.w: He wore me like a silken knot,

notes.n: A glove is replaceable: casual cruelty of the upper class.
notes.w: He changed me like a glove;

notes.n: Society’s view of a ‘fallen woman’: dehumanised (‘thing’), morally polluted. Biblical language of uncleanness.
notes.w: an unclean thing,

notes.n: The **dove** symbolises purity, peace and the Holy Spirit: what she has lost. Conditional ‘might have been’ = regret.
notes.w: Who might have been a dove.

stanzas.label: Stanza 3: Kate chosen
lines: O Lady Kate, my cousin Kate,
You grew more fair than I:
He saw you at your father's gate,
Chose you, and cast me by.
He watched your steps along the lane,
Your work among the rye;
He lifted you from mean estate
To sit with him on high.

notes.n: **Apostrophe**: she now addresses Kate directly. ‘Lady’ (her new title) beside ‘cousin’ (family) shows the conflict: same origins, now unequal. Possibly sarcastic.
notes.w: O Lady Kate, my cousin Kate,

notes.n: Verbs of control belong to the lord: women are chosen or discarded like goods. Caesura splits the two fates.
notes.w: Chose you, and cast me by.

notes.n: The lord’s **predatory gaze** is repeated from stanza 1: Kate is being hunted in the same way.
notes.w: He watched your steps along the lane,

notes.n: ‘Mean estate’ = low social class. Marriage is the only route up for a working woman: **class mobility through men**.
notes.w: He lifted you from mean estate

notes.n: Height imagery: Kate rises as the speaker falls. The ‘fall’ links to Eve and the language of the ‘fallen woman’.
notes.w: To sit with him on high.

stanzas.label: Stanza 4: double standards
lines: Because you were so good and pure
He bound you with his ring:
The neighbours call you good and pure,
Call me an outcast thing.
Even so I sit and howl in dust,
You sit in gold and sing:
Now which of us has tenderer heart?
You had the stronger wing.

notes.n: **Sarcasm**: Kate kept her virginity, so she got marriage. Repeated two lines later as the neighbours’ judgement, exposing **society’s hypocrisy**.
notes.w: Because you were so good and pure

notes.n: ‘Bound’ suggests marriage is a form of captivity too: Kate is not free either. Grade 9 point: both women are controlled.
notes.w: He bound you with his ring:

notes.n: Dehumanising noun again (‘thing’), now from the neighbours: the speaker is socially excluded.
notes.w: an outcast thing.

notes.n: **Antithesis** with the next line: dust (poverty, mourning, biblical death) vs gold (wealth). ‘Howl’ is animalistic despair.
notes.w: Even so I sit and howl in dust,

notes.n: Parallel syntax ‘I sit… You sit’ makes the injustice stark. Singing = contentment, perhaps like a caged bird.
notes.w: You sit in gold and sing:

notes.n: Rhetorical question challenging the reader’s moral judgement: who is really ‘good’?
notes.w: Now which of us has tenderer heart?

notes.n: Bird **metaphor**: Kate was stronger, or more calculating, flying higher. Links back to the lost ‘dove’.
notes.w: You had the stronger wing.

stanzas.label: Stanza 5: the speaker’s claim
lines: O cousin Kate, my love was true,
Your love was writ in sand:
If he had fooled not me but you,
If you stood where I stand,
He'd not have won me with his love
Nor bought me with his land;
I would have spit into his face
And not have taken his hand.

notes.n: **Metaphor**: Kate’s love is shallow and temporary (washed away). The speaker claims moral superiority: her love was ‘true’.
notes.w: Your love was writ in sand:

notes.n: **Hypothetical** role reversal: shows how arbitrary the women’s fates were.
notes.w: If you stood where I stand,

notes.n: Marriage presented as a **transaction**: Kate was ‘bought’. A sharp critique of Victorian marriage and wealth.
notes.w: Nor bought me with his land;

notes.n: Shockingly **violent, unladylike** language for a Victorian woman’s voice: anger and defiance. The tone has shifted from lament to fury.
notes.w: I would have spit into his face

stanzas.label: Stanza 6: the son as triumph
lines: Yet I've a gift you have not got,
And seem not like to get:
For all your clothes and wedding-ring
I've little doubt you fret.
My fair-haired son, my shame, my pride,
Cling closer, closer yet:
Your father would give lands for one
To wear his coronet.

notes.n: **Volta**: ‘Yet’ turns the poem from loss to triumph. The ‘gift’ is her son; Kate is childless.
notes.w: Yet I've a gift you have not got,

notes.n: Smug, taunting tone: she imagines Kate’s anxiety. Revenge through words.
notes.w: I've little doubt you fret.

notes.n: **Antithesis/oxymoron**: the son is evidence of her ‘sin’ but also her greatest joy. Sums up the conflict of the poem.
notes.w: my shame, my pride,

notes.n: **Repetition**: protective love; she holds him like a possession the lord cannot have.
notes.w: Cling closer, closer yet:

notes.n: Her son is illegitimate so cannot inherit: the lord has land but no heir. Irony: the lord lacks what she has.
notes.w: Your father would give lands for one

notes.n: Ends on power and status: the coronet (a noble’s crown). Her final weapon is the child. A defiant, ambiguous ending: triumph or bitterness?
notes.w: To wear his coronet.

summary: Cousin Kate (1862) is Christina Rossetti’s dramatic monologue spoken by a ‘fallen woman’ who was seduced and abandoned by a lord who then married her cousin; compare how it presents conflict between women, class and gender power, betrayal and defiance, with Victorian context.

terms.d: Victorian term for a woman who had lost her ‘virtue’ through sex outside marriage.
Directly addressing a person who is absent or cannot reply (‘O Lady Kate’).
A narrative song-like poem, often about love and betrayal.
A turn in the poem’s argument or tone (‘Yet’).
A rule applied more strictly to one group (women) than another (men).
Contrasting ideas in balanced phrases (dust/gold, shame/pride).
